summary: Deep technical session focused on strategies to serve extremely long contexts (800k-1M tokens) for Valen Med's longitudinal patient records use case. Discussed KV-sharding across GPUs, block-sparse and sliding-window attention, quantization tradeoffs, runtime memory offload, RDMA/InfiniBand networking considerations for on-prem, and realistic latency vs cost targets. Agreed to run a Redwood Dedicated benchmark with customer's sample corpus and follow up on networking and security requirements.
topics: Sharded KV cache architectures (per-GPU vs distributed index)
Chunking and hierarchical retrieval for 1M token contexts
Sparse attention patterns (block-sparse, sliding window, LSH variants)
Quantization at scale (4-bit, mixed-precision) and perf/regression risks
Batching policies and deterministic latency SLOs
On-prem/VPC networking: RDMA/InfiniBand, PCIe, and cross-host KV coherence
Security/compliance for Private deployment (KMS/HSM, audit logs)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna deep dive into the long context plan, especially around 800k to 1M token workflows. Priya and I will walk through architectural patterns and tradeoffs.
[00:18] Dr. Maya Singh: Thanks Alex. To set context — our clinical timeline per patient is roughly 600k tokens on average and heavy cases push near a million. Need low-ish tail latency for interactive analyst queries, and we also run batch scoring overnight.
[00:36] Alex Chen: Got it. Priya, do you want to start with how we think about KV distribution for these scales?
[00:42] Priya Natarajan: Sure. So first, you can think of the KV as the working memory for autoregressive decoding. At 1M tokens the naive approach to keep full KV in a single device is impossible. The patterns we usually consider: per-GPU sharded KV with local attention windows, or a distributed index where KV rows live on different hosts and are fetched on demand. Each has tradeoffs.
[01:05] Ethan Park: When you say fetched on demand, are we talking PCIe pulls or network RPCs? That's a big latency variable.
[01:11] Priya Natarajan: Both are possible. For Dedicated / on-prem we'd aim for NVLink / NVSwitch intra-node sharding to keep most fetches local. For cross-node you need RDMA or very low latency RPCs — InfiniBand is ideal. If you have to go to CPU over PCIe, we see big tail latency spikes.
[01:30] Dr. Maya Singh: For Valen we're hoping to avoid cross-host round trips for typical analyst queries. How realistic is that?
[01:36] Priya Natarajan: It depends on how you chunk and route requests. If you pre-route queries to the subset of shards that contain the patient history — for instance, hash by patient id — then most requests hit a small number of GPUs. Also prefix/KV caching at the application layer helps: keep the most-recently-accessed segments warm on local GPU.
[01:56] Alex Chen: I'll add that Redwood's runtime supports automatic prefix caching and eviction policies; we can expose heuristics like LRU, TTL-based and size-based evictions.
[02:05] Dr. Maya Singh: How about chunking strategy? We've experimented with sliding windows but we worry about coherence across windows for attention.
[02:12] Priya Natarajan: Right. There are a few patterns: sliding window (overlapping windows), hierarchical chunking where you compress older context into summaries and keep detailed KV for recent segments, and sparse global attention where you only allow long-range attention to a subset of tokens. Each increases complexity. Hierarchical chunking often gives the best compromise: you index fine-grained recent segments and a compressed representation for distant history.
[02:36] Ethan Park: Compression — are we talking learned embeddings or something like vector sketches?
[02:40] Priya Natarajan: Could be both. For retrieval we use dense embeddings and an ANN index; for attention-aware compression you can use learned summary vectors stored in KV so attention can reference them cheaply. But beware drift: summaries can miss salient events, so we tie summaries to eval sets.
[02:57] Lena Ortiz: You mentioned sparse attention variants — which ones are production-ready? BigBird-like, Longformer? Or more experimental LSH?
[03:04] Priya Natarajan: Block-sparse and sliding-window patterns (Longformer/BigBird style) are fairly battle-tested. LSH/FlashAttention hybrids are promising but can be brittle across sequence lengths. Our runtime supports optimized FlashAttention kernels for contiguous chunks and block-sparse attention for very long sequences. We also have fallback kernels when sequence shapes change.
[03:24] Dr. Maya Singh: What about quantization — can we quantize to 4-bit at that scale to save memory?
[03:29] Priya Natarajan: Mixed. 4-bit (QLoRA-style) quantization reduces memory a lot, but you must validate generation quality over your clinical prompts. For very long KV we often use mixed precision: keep KV keys/values in 8-bit or 16-bit and quantize weights to 4-bit. Also per-layer calibration is important — certain layers are more sensitive. We can run regression tests during benchmark.
[03:51] Alex Chen: To add a practical datapoint: in our internal tests, a 7B-ish model with 4-bit weights and 8-bit KV cut memory footprint ~45%, but some rare prompts showed hallucination increases — that's why evals tied to customer prompts are critical.
[04:07] Ethan Park: On runtime offload — is it feasible to page KV to NVMe non-blocking? We have large NVMe on our nodes.
[04:13] Priya Natarajan: NVMe offload is viable for cold KV segments. The challenge is throughput and deterministic latency: NVMe brings acceptable bandwidth for background batch jobs but tail latency for interactive queries can spike. PMEM (persistent memory) and DAX mode can reduce overhead, and async prefetch with predictive caching works well. We also support checkpointing KV shards to NVMe to warm them up for scheduled queries.
[04:36] Dr. Maya Singh: So for interactive SLOs we should avoid NVMe for hot segments and reserve it for cold archival?
[04:41] Priya Natarajan: Exactly. Keep hot segments in GPU memory or host RAM with RDMA-accessible mounts; use NVMe for cold/backfill.
[04:48] Alex Chen: Let's talk numbers. What latency should you expect for a 1M context query if most KV hits are local?
[04:55] Priya Natarajan: If you front-load the request to only 2-4 GPUs and you have NVLink intra-node, we can hit p50 in ~150-300ms for short generations and p95 around 400-800ms depending on batch size and quantization. If you need full cross-host fanout to many shards, p95 can go to multiple seconds. Those are rough — we'll validate with the benchmark.
[05:17] Dr. Maya Singh: That's in line with our target. Cost-wise, what's the delta between keeping everything on GPUs vs heavy offload?
[05:23] Alex Chen: GPUs are the fixed cost driver. Dedicated with 8-16 GPUs will be significantly more expensive than a mixed CPU/GPU approach, but it gives the lowest and most consistent latency. Offload saves GPU memory but increases infra complexity and unpredictable tails.
[05:36] Ethan Park: About batching — we need deterministic latency for interactive explorers, but also high throughput for batch scoring. Can Redwood separate routes?
[05:43] Priya Natarajan: Yes, we recommend separate routes and autoscale policies. One route with small batch sizes and stricter latency SLO, another for batched scoring that can accept larger batches and lower priority. Runtime-level QoS ensures burst isolation.
[05:56] Dr. Maya Singh: Security and compliance — we're required to keep PHI within our VPC and integrate KMS. How does Private deployment handle key management?
[06:03] Alex Chen: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS integration and HSM passthrough for key operations. Audit logs and token-level tracing are stored in your control plane inside the VPC; we can configure retention windows as needed. We also support SAML/SSO for RBAC.
[06:17] Lena Ortiz: For an on-prem cluster, what do you need network-wise?
[06:20] Priya Natarajan: Preferably a fat-tree with RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) or InfiniBand for cross-node KV fetches. NVLink/NVSwitch is ideal intra-node. PCIe 4.0/5.0 and top-tier NVMe are helpful for paging. Also ensure low jitter on the fabric — that matters more than raw bandwidth for tail latency.
[06:39] Ethan Park: We have a Mellanox-based InfiniBand fabric in our staging cluster. Is that enough?
[06:44] Priya Natarajan: Yes, that's exactly the hardware we look for. We'll want to test RDMA performance with your dataset.
[06:50] Alex Chen: There's sometimes confusion on consistency when you shard KV across hosts — how does Redwood ensure correctness for autoregressive decoding?
[06:57] Priya Natarajan: We enforce a causal ordering and deterministic merge step for KV fetches. If a request needs tokens from multiple shards, we fetch in parallel and apply a deterministic merge. For speed we try to minimize the number of shard boundaries touched. We also support sticky routing to keep recovery deterministic.
[07:17] Dr. Maya Singh: Any considerations for model architecture itself — should we prefer certain model families for extreme context?
[07:22] Priya Natarajan: Encoder-decoder hybrids sometimes offer advantages for retrieval-augmented flows, but autoregressive decoders with optimized attention kernels are the easiest to scale. Models built with more modular attention (e.g., local + global tokens) can be more memory-efficient. We'll review your model candidates in the benchmark.
[07:38] Ethan Park: Regarding evals — you mentioned regression checks. How does Redwood tie generation regressions to quantization or kernel changes?
[07:45] Alex Chen: Our Redwood Optimize pipeline can run diff-evals: we re-run a curated prompt set (customer-provided) across variants and surface token-level deltas and semantic metrics. We can gate rollouts based on thresholds you set.
[07:57] Dr. Maya Singh: Great. For the benchmark, can we confirm what Redwood will run?
[08:01] Priya Natarajan: We'll run: (1) an end-to-end live query test with your sample corpus targeted at 800k-1M tokens per subject, (2) a synthetic stress test that fans out to many shards to measure tail latency, (3) nightly batch scoring throughput test with NVMe backfill to simulate cold data. We'll collect p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, network metrics, and memory hot/cold hit rates.
[08:23] Lena Ortiz: What logs and artifacts will you share after the run?
[08:26] Alex Chen: Raw perf logs, summary dashboards, flamegraphs, and a short recommendations doc with tuning knobs (batch sizes, eviction TTLs, quantization layers). We can also produce a candidate roadmap for Private deployment.
[08:37] Dr. Maya Singh: One last practical question: are there known failure modes we should prepare for?
[08:41] Priya Natarajan: Yes — common ones are: (1) sudden cluster-wide tail latency due to a hot-spoted shard, (2) regressions after aggressive quantization on sensitive layers, (3) network jitter causing inter-node fetch stalls. We mitigate with circuit breakers, canary rollouts, and push-button fallbacks to lower-context modes.
[09:00] Ethan Park: Could you give an example fallback?
[09:03] Priya Natarajan: If the distributed KV fetch latency exceeds threshold, we fall back to a compressed-history mode where we only load a compressed summary for distant history and full detail for the most recent N tokens. That keeps latency bounded but slightly reduces fidelity.
[09:17] Alex Chen: All right let's recap next steps...
[09:20] [crosstalk] Dr. Maya Singh: Thanks, this is super helpful.
[09:22] Alex Chen: Recap: Redwood runs dedicated benchmark on 1M token patterns, Valen provides sample corpus, schedule networking deep-dive, and we share security artifacts. We'll follow up with calendar invites.
[09:34] Ethan Park: Cool. Quick note — there were a few spots in the test where model names got garbled in our earlier docs, so please call out exact Docker images and kernel versions in the runbook.
[09:44] Priya Natarajan: Will do. We'll include exact image tags, CUDA, NCCL, and kernel versions.
[09:49] Lena Ortiz: Appreciate it, thanks everyone.
[09:51] Alex Chen: Thanks all, we'll send the summary and action items after the call. Bye.

Notes: occasional transcription errors present (e.g., "kay vee" for KV, "roce" transcribed as "rose" in places). Links mentioned: (1) benchmark template deck — shared in chat, (2) security checklist doc — to be attached to follow-up email.
